transcript.text: Samsung WW90T534DAW keeps coming up with 4C after a couple of minutes. Drum is dry. Any ideas before I call someone out?

Yes, there's a fair chance you can sort this yourself. On Samsung washing machines 4C means a water supply fault: the machine opened its fill valve but little or no water came in within the time it allows. With a dry drum, that fits perfectly. In order of likelihood it's usually the supply (tap partly off or hose kinked), then a blocked mesh filter where the fill hose screws onto the back, and only after those are ruled out the inlet (fill) valve itself. 1. Check the household supply: run a cold tap in the kitchen. If the flow is weak or nothing comes out, the problem is the property supply, not the machine.
2. Check the tap the machine is plumbed into is turned fully on (lever in line with the pipe, or the knob fully anticlockwise), and that the fill hose behind the machine isn't kinked or squashed against the wall. Found it off or kinked? Sort it and try again.
3. Clean the inlet mesh: switch off and unplug the machine, turn the tap off and put a towel down. Unscrew the fill hose from the back of the machine and look into the inlet; there's a small mesh filter that clogs with grit or scale. If you can, ease it out with pliers, rinse it under the tap and refit it (some Samsungs also have a mesh in the tap end of the hose). Refit the hose hand-tight, turn the tap on, check for drips, then run a short programme.
4. While the hose is off, you can point it into a bucket and briefly open the tap to confirm water flows strongly through it. If the supply is strong, the tap is open, the hose is clear and the mesh is clean, but it still won't take water and shows 4C, the inlet valve becomes the likely culprit. That's when an engineer visit (or a valve replacement, if you're confident) makes sense. Let me know what you find with the taps and the mesh.
Kitchen cold tap pressure is normal. The machine's tap was open (turned it fully anticlockwise anyway, no change) and the hose isn't kinked. I'll check the mesh filter next.

That's a good result. The tap fully open and no kink, we've ruled out the supply side. That leaves two realistic causes. The inlet mesh is still the most likely, especially if the machine has filled more slowly over recent weeks. The inlet valve itself comes second. 1. Mesh blocked with grit or scale: clean it, refit it and run a short programme. If it fills and the 4C doesn't come back, that was it. Hard-water areas often clog it again over time, so it's worth checking now and then.
2. Mesh already clean: give the hose the bucket test (briefly open the tap with the hose end in a bucket). Strong flow means the water is reaching the machine fine, so the fault is past that point. That points to the inlet valve.
3. Before the retest, close the door firmly and listen when you start a programme. You should hear the door lock click, then a few seconds later a click or faint hum from the top back as the valve opens. If it never seems to get as far as trying, the problem is more likely on the control side, and that's an engineer job. If it does come down to the inlet valve, it's a fairly common and not too expensive repair. It's normally reached by taking the top panel off, so an engineer is the sensible route unless you're confident with that sort of job. Let me know what the mesh looks like.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the fill-hose mesh filter is" — A small mesh filter sits inside the fill-hose connector at the tap/valve end and catches grit. Turn the tap off, unscrew the hose and rinse the mesh. Typical layout — your machine may differ.]

Took the hose off and the mesh filter was clogged with grey grit and limescale bits. Cleaned it and refitted, now it fills normally and the 4C has gone. Also heard a faint buzz from the back earlier when it should've been filling. Water company was working in the street two days ago and the water ran brown briefly, if that's relevant.

[Heading: Likely cause: filter]
The water company work is very relevant. When they work on the mains it stirs up sediment, which is why the water ran brown, and that grey grit gets carried along until it hits the first fine mesh, which here was your machine's inlet filter. It blocked the flow, the machine timed out waiting for water, and you got 4C. The faint buzz fits the same picture. The inlet valve was opening and straining against a blocked inlet, which is a common knock-on effect. Now that it fills normally, the buzz should be gone or much quieter. If a loud buzz while filling ever comes back with a clean mesh, the valve would be worth looking at, but nothing suggests that now. 1. If the water company works in your street again, or the water runs discoloured, run the kitchen cold tap until it's clear before using the washing machine or dishwasher. That flushes the grit out before it reaches their filters.
2. Over the next wash or two, glance at the hose connection on the back to make sure it's dry. A washer that isn't quite seated after refitting can weep slightly. Hand-tight is enough. It's worth checking that mesh once or twice a year anyway if you're in a hard-water area. Is there anything else I can help with?

plan: They asked: "Any ideas before I call someone out?" - answer that first.
Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Samsung; model WW90T534DAW; code 4C.
The fault they reported is: "error 4C after a couple of minutes". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.

Explain what the error code means using ERROR CODES. If ERROR CODES does not resolve it, say plainly that you cannot confirm what it means on their model (it may not be an error code at all, for example part of the model name), never guess a meaning, and work from the symptoms.
